claim: The search identified 3082 articles from database inception to 24 November 2022.
source: We searched PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) from inception up to 24.11.2022
evidence: The manuscript text states the search date and Figure 1 shows the PRISMA flowchart with 3082 articles identified.

claim: After deduplication, 1837 articles remained for title and abstract screening.
source: The search identified 3082 articles, which decreased to 1837 after deduplication.
evidence: The text states this number and Figure 1 shows the deduplication process.

claim: 42 studies qualified for inclusion in the systematic review.
source: A total of 488 studies were eligible for full-text review, of which 41 studies qualified for inclusion. The screening of the citations of the 41 studies identified one additional eligible study (Appendix 11 section 2), for a total of 42 studies, 40 RCTs, and two quasi-RCTs
evidence: The text explicitly states 42 studies were included and Figure 1 shows this in the PRISMA flowchart.

claim: 29 studies including 5054 patients qualified for statistical analysis.
source: 42 trials were eligible and 29, including 5054 patients, qualified for statistical analysis.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this number of studies and patients.

claim: 13 studies were excluded from meta-analysis due to zero events in both treatment arms.
source: Twenty-nine studies could be included in the meta-analysis; 13 were excluded due to zero events in both treatment arms.
evidence: The text explicitly states the reason for exclusion of 13 studies.

claim: The included studies were published between 1977 and 2021.
source: The included studies were published between 1977 and 2021, with a median publication year of 1995 and few recent studies (Figure 2A).
evidence: The text states the publication year range and Figure 2A shows the distribution.

claim: The median publication year of included studies was 1995.
source: The included studies were published between 1977 and 2021, with a median publication year of 1995 and few recent studies (Figure 2A).
evidence: The text explicitly states the median and Figure 2A shows a red vertical line indicating the median.

claim: Only 9 studies (21%) explicitly defined a resistance outcome.
source: The development of antibiotic resistance was typically not the main outcome: only nine studies (21%) explicitly defined a resistance outcome (Supplementary file 1, Appendix 3—table 1).
evidence: The text explicitly provides this count and percentage.

claim: 22 studies (52%) focused on a specific pathogen species or pathogen group.
source: Twenty-two (52%) focused on a specific pathogen species (resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli, H. pylori, Mtb, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus), or pathogen group (MAC, Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serotype Thyphi, or Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serotype Parthypi A).
evidence: The text explicitly states this number and percentage.

claim: Only 2 of all 42 studies had a low overall risk of bias for the outcome acquisition of resistance.
source: For the outcome acquisition of resistance, only two of all 42 studies had a low overall risk of bias according to the risk of bias assessment.
evidence: The text explicitly states the risk of bias assessment results.

claim: 12 studies (29%) were at high risk of bias.
source: Twelve (29%) were at high risk of bias, 28 (67%) at moderate risk of bias (Appendix 3).
evidence: The text explicitly provides this count and percentage.

claim: 28 studies (67%) were at moderate risk of bias.
source: Twelve (29%) were at high risk of bias, 28 (67%) at moderate risk of bias (Appendix 3).
evidence: The text explicitly provides this count and percentage.

claim: The overall pooled odds ratio for acquisition of resistance comparing higher versus lower number of antibiotics was 1.23 (95% CI 0.68–2.25).
source: The overall pooled OR for acquisition of resistance comparing a lower number of antibiotics versus a higher one was 1.23 (95% CI 0.68–2.25), with substantial heterogeneity between studies (I2=77.4%).
evidence: The text states this result and Figure 3 shows the forest plot with this pooled estimate.

claim: There was substantial heterogeneity between studies for acquisition of resistance (I2=77.4%).
source: The overall pooled OR for acquisition of resistance comparing a lower number of antibiotics versus a higher one was 1.23 (95% CI 0.68–2.25), with substantial heterogeneity between studies (I2=77.4%).
evidence: The text explicitly reports the I2 statistic indicating heterogeneity.

claim: The pooled odds ratio for de novo emergence of resistance was 0.74 (95% CI 0.34–1.59).
source: The latter OR was compatible with the OR for de novo emergence of resistance (pooled OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.34–1.59; I2=77%).
evidence: The text explicitly states this pooled estimate.

claim: For H. pylori, a higher number of antibiotics performed better than a lower number (pooled OR 0.14, 95% CI 0.03–0.55; I2=41.7%).
source: Stratified analyses revealed that a higher number of antibiotics performed better than a lower number in the case of H. pylori, (pooled OR 0.14, 95% CI 0.03–0.55; I2=41.7%, Figure 3A)
evidence: The text states this result and Figure 3A shows the stratified analysis for H. pylori.

claim: For MAC, a higher number of antibiotics performed better than a lower number (pooled OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.06–0.52; I2=26.8%).
source: Stratified analyses revealed that a higher number of antibiotics performed better than a lower number in the case of H. pylori, (pooled OR 0.14, 95% CI 0.03–0.55; I2=41.7%, Figure 3A), and MAC (pooled OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.06–0.52; I2=26.8%, Figure 3A)
evidence: The text states this result and Figure 3A shows the stratified analysis for MAC.

claim: When treatment arms had no antibiotics in common, a lower number of antibiotics performed better (pooled OR 4.73, 95% CI 2.14–10.42; I2=37%).
source: Furthermore, a lower number of antibiotics performed better than a higher number if the compared treatment arms had no antibiotics in common (pooled OR 4.73, 95% CI 2.14–10.42; I2=37%, Appendix 6—table 1)
evidence: The text explicitly states this subgroup analysis result.

claim: When restricting analysis to studies with at least one common antibiotic, there was a weak indication that a higher number of antibiotics performs better (pooled OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.28–1.07; I2=74%).
source: In contrast, when restricting the analysis to studies with at least one common antibiotic in the treatment arms we found no evidence of a difference, only a weak indication that a higher number of antibiotics performs better (pooled OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.28–1.07; I2=74%, Figure 3B).
evidence: The text states this result and Figure 3B shows the forest plot for this subgroup.

claim: When considering only resistance measurements of antibiotics common to both treatment arms, the arm with a higher number of antibiotics shows a benefit (pooled OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.18–0.81; I2=75%).
source: When considering only resistance measurements of antibiotics common to both treatment arms instead of all resistance measurements, the arm with a higher number of antibiotics shows a benefit in comparison to the one with fewer (pooled OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.18–0.81; I2=75%, Appendix 6 section viii.).
evidence: The text explicitly states this subgroup analysis result.

claim: If the study measured acquisition of resistance of both gram-negative and positive bacteria, fewer antibiotics performed better (pooled OR 3.38, 95% CI 1.08–10.58; I2=38.35%).
source: If the study measured the acquisition of resistance of both gram-negative and positive bacteria, fewer antibiotics performed better (pooled OR 3.38, 95% CI 1.08–10.58; I2=38.35%, Appendix 6 section vi.).
evidence: The text explicitly states this subgroup analysis result.

claim: The probability of alterations of prescribed treatment due to adverse events was higher using more antibiotics compared to fewer (pooled OR 1.61, 95% CI 1.12–2.31; I2=5%).
source: The probability of the secondary outcome 'alterations of the prescribed treatment due to adverse events,' was higher using more antibiotics in comparison to fewer (pooled OR 1.61, 95% CI 1.12–2.31; I2=5%; Appendix 9 section v.).
evidence: The text explicitly states this secondary outcome result.

claim: In 15 studies (36%), the proportion of patients with alterations of prescribed treatment due to adverse events was reported.
source: In 15 studies (36%), the proportion of patients with alterations of the prescribed treatment due to adverse events was reported, with three studies (20%) reporting zero cases in both treatment arms.
evidence: The text explicitly provides this count and percentage.

claim: 23 of the included studies (55%) compared treatment arms with at least one administered antibiotic in common.
source: Twenty-three of the included studies (55%) compared treatment arms with at least one administered antibiotic in common; the remaining studies compared treatment arms with no overlap in administered antibiotics (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this count and percentage.

claim: 19 studies (45%) compared treatment arms with no antibiotics in common.
source: 19 (45%) of our included studies compared treatment arms with no antibiotics in common
evidence: The text explicitly states this count and percentage.

claim: 22 studies (52%) had more than one antibiotic not identical in the treatment arms.
source: 19 (45%) of our included studies compared treatment arms with no antibiotics in common, and 22 studies (52%) had more than one antibiotic not identical in the treatment arms (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this count and percentage.

claim: Most studies did not have statistical power to detect differences in within-patient resistance development even assuming large effects.
source: Consequently, most studies did not have the statistical power to detect differences in within-patient resistance development even if we assume that the effect on resistance development is large between treatment arms (Figure 2B, Appendix 8).
evidence: The text states this and Figure 2B shows the calculated statistical power of included studies.

claim: Antibiotic combination therapy is the standard of care for H. pylori, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Mycobacterium leprae.
source: Importantly, it is the standard of care for some bacterial pathogens, such as H. pylori, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), or Mycobacterium leprae (Alemu Belachew and Naafs, 2019; De Francesco et al., 2017; Singh et al., 2020).

claim: The simultaneous occurrence of resistance mutations to multiple drugs is less likely than resistance to single drugs.
source: The simultaneous occurrence of resistance mutations to multiple drugs is less likely than resistance to single drugs.

claim: Combination therapy should reduce the development of resistance according to theoretical expectations.
source: Combination therapy should, therefore, reduce the development of resistance (Bonhoeffer et al., 1997).

claim: This expectation is supported by viral infections such as HIV, where multiple point mutations are required for resistance to combination antiviral therapy.
source: This expectation is supported by viral infections such as HIV, where multiple point mutations are required for resistance to combination antiviral therapy.
